strengths: UNOT addresses a useful amortized optimal transport problem. Combining Fourier neural operators, adversarially generated measures, and bootstrapped supervision is a meaningful contribution toward reusing one initializer across datasets and grid resolutions.

The initialization results are promising across six within- and cross-dataset settings, evaluated over 500 samples. Table 1 reports substantial iteration reductions, while Table 2 shows approximately 2.75–3.4× speedups on the 64×64 datasets.

The appendix strengthens the evaluation with resolution sweeps, an epsilon-conditioned variant, and marginal-violation curves. Architecture details, hyperparameters, training resources, and a code/model-weights link support reproducibility.

Predicting one potential and constructing supervision through a few Sinkhorn refinements is well motivated. Proposition 5 provides a principled residual-to-error relationship under its positive-kernel and normalization assumptions.
weaknesses: The advertised generator universality is not established for the implemented model. Appendix C uses 200 latent dimensions to generate 8192 outputs and explicitly does not enforce the required Lipschitz constraint. These departures invalidate applying Theorem 3 to the trained generator. Moreover, Corollary 4 is false as stated: G2(z)=ReLU(z/2) and G1(z)=ReLU(1+z/2) satisfy its component assumptions, but G1(G2(z)) is always at least 1, excluding positive density on (0,1). This undermines a principal theoretical contribution.

The OT definitions and learning targets require reconciliation. Equation (1)'s negative KL sign appears to be a correctable error. More substantially, Proposition 1 identifies entropy-reference scaling potentials with the KL-reference potentials of equation (3), omitting the marginal factors in their relationship. Proposition 2 consequently does not directly establish convergence of the actual learned targets. Algorithm 1 also reports only the transport cost, whereas the defined OT objective includes regularization, leaving the experimental metric and its relationship to later Sinkhorn-divergence calculations ambiguous.

The state-of-the-art claim lacks decisive comparisons and ablations. Amos et al. is excluded based on asserted out-of-distribution failure without a controlled comparison; fixed-resolution experiments using the same synthetic training data would be informative. There are also no quantitative ablations isolating adversarial generation or bootstrapping against nonadversarial synthetic sampling and dual-objective training. The results therefore establish gains over the reported conventional initializers more clearly than the necessity or comparative advantage of the proposed training design.

The downstream geometry claims rely mainly on qualitative examples, including a single displayed GeONet comparison. More seriously, Algorithm 3 applies softmax directly to the probability vector minus its gradient. This is neither Euclidean simplex projection nor the usual mirror-descent update, which uses log probabilities. It can move a nonuniform optimum even when the gradient is constant across coordinates. The algorithm needs correction or clarification, together with aggregate barycenter and geodesic accuracy measurements, before these conclusions are convincing.

Proposition 5 supports vanishing-residual consistency, but the wording that bootstrapping 'provably minimizes' ground-truth loss is stronger than the result. An upper bound does not establish equivalent minimizers within a restricted network class or convergence of the stopped-gradient adversarial updates. Its kernel-dependent constant can also become extremely large at small epsilon; the paper does not assess whether it provides informative finite-error control in the experimental regime.

The practical acceleration evidence has limits. Timing comparisons use 1% transport-cost error; although Figure 14 reports feasibility residuals, runtimes at matched marginal or primal-dual tolerances are missing. Gaussian-initialization timings are omitted, and MNIST is slower with UNOT (0.61× in Table 2). These qualifications matter when interpreting the broader solver-acceleration claim.
